dimensionExamples.example: Players can form premade parties with friends before entering a match

dimension.title: Party Creation
dimension.description: Party Creation encompasses all games where groups are defined by the players themselves prior to initiating gameplay, typically leveraging friend lists or co-located party creation.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can queue up solo or with others, and the game matches them into teams based on their rank

dimension.title: Looking for Group
dimension.description: Looking for Group happens when there are grouping mechanisms that allow players to formally look for and create a group/party. This is typically achieved through matchmaking or looking for group queues.

dimensionExamples.example: Teams share the overarching goal of destroying the enemy Nexus while achieving secondary objectives like capturing towers, dragons, and Baron Nashor

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimensionExamples.example: While the end goal is shared, individual roles like top laner, support and jungler have specific objectives that depend on each other

dimension.title: Intertwined
dimension.description: Intertwined goals determine individual objectives assigned to different players that, in some way, are dependent on each other. The dependency may be uni- or bidirectional. If the dependency is bidirectional, goals are interdependent.

dimensionExamples.example: In League of Legends, progress during a match is shared among the team. Players work together to achieve objectives like taking down towers, slaying dragons, and eventually destroying the enemy Nexus

dimension.title: Party
dimension.description: Party progression results from the contributions of a group of players that opted to play together, where part of the progress is solely associated with that group (not shared with the rest of the server or community).

dimensionExamples.example: Each player controls a unique champion with distinct abilities and responsibilities in the game

dimension.title: Individual
dimension.description: Individual progression is defined by individual choice and the individual impact of the progression. In-game activities can vary from individual to fully cooperative but progression affects the individual.

dimensionExamples.example: Each champion has distinct abilities, strengths, and roles within the team, making individual contributions unique

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimensionExamples.example: Each player controls a single unique champion

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct means that each player controls a different entity or set of entities

dimensionExamples.example: The champion pool refers to the set of champions available to all players, which they can select before starting the game

dimension.title: Pool
dimension.description: Pool describes when players are given an array of playable entities to choose from (e.g. characters, nations, class). These have predefined gameplay characteristics and in some cases, players can be forced to have a unique selection.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can customize their gameplay through runes, summoner spells, and item builds

dimension.title: Customisable
dimension.description: Customisable encompasses all games with upgrades, levelling systems, and others that give players the ability to create and modify their representation throughout the game.

dimensionExamples.example: Five players form a team and work together, usually comprising different roles like top lane, mid lane, jungle, bottom, and support

dimension.title: Teammates
dimension.description: Teammates, where players within a team need to coordinate their actions, abilities, and roles in order to reach a common goal against at least another team.

dimensionExamples.example: The opposing team of five players, who aim to defeat your team and destroy your Nexus

dimension.title: Competitors
dimension.description: Competitors, where you may be able to compete with other players, either momentarily or through the whole game session (e.g. team vs team match-based games).

dimensionExamples.example: The map is the same for everyone in the game

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimensionExamples.example: Objectives like dragons, Baron Nashor, and map vision are shared tasks for the team

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared is when there is a single viewpoint that both players share. Typically, this happens when players are co-located. All Shared Player Views are, by definition, in Shared Game Worlds.

dimensionExamples.example: Each player has specific tasks based on their role, such as farming, warding, or initiating fights, and these are distinct from other teammates

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: Players must synchronize their abilities and actions, such as coordinating ultimates or setting up crowd control for team fights

dimension.title: Coupled Collaboration
dimension.description: In coupled collaboration, players take on different tasks that somehow intertwine and typically contribute to a shared outcome.

dimensionExamples.example: Players often engage in simultaneous actions towards a common goal, like pushing lanes or securing objectives, even if they're performing different tasks in parallel

dimension.title: Coincident Collaboration
dimension.description: In coincident collaboration, players are accomplishing the same task together.

dimensionExamples.example: While progressing through the game, teammates must cooperate simultaneously to secure objectives, defend their base, or win team fights

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can use pings, text chat, or emotes, but is entirely up to them, and the game doesn’t require or impose any specific method of communication to achieve objectives

dimension.title: Agnostic
dimension.description: When Agnostic, the game is neutral to player communication, it does not incentivise nor it places any restrictions. It is the only communication design that does not promote cooperation.

dimensionExamples.example: There's a text chat where you can text your teammates and even the enemies

dimension.title: Text Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using text

dimensionExamples.example: There's a ping system to quickly alert teammates

dimension.title: Pings
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate by signaling specific things in their view (e.g. aiming at something and signaling)

dimensionExamples.example: There's emotes to express your present feelings

dimension.title: Emotes
dimension.description: Players can communicate through particular animations their characters have (e.g. pointing at something)

dimensionExamples.example: Communicating through the use of abilities, to insinuate something like the start of a team fight

dimension.title: In-Game Movement/Actions
dimension.description: Players can communicate through specific movement or actions (e.g. shooting a weapon on the ground to notify others to pick it up)

dimensionExamples.example: Players often rely on each other to complete objectives effectively. For example, a support player may need to protect the ADC (Attack Damage Carry) while they farm minions, and the ADC relies on the support for vision and crowd control during fights

dimension.title: Task
dimension.description: Task refers to gameplay tasks where at least one player is dependent on another. These can force players to coordinate to be effective and complete them.

dimensionExamples.example: Players often group together to secure objectives and engage in team fights

dimension.title: Grouping
dimension.description: Grouping refers to activities that require a certain number of players to be accessed/completed.

dimensionExamples.example: Supports and other champions provide heals, shields, buffs, and crowd control effects to assist their teammates

dimension.title: Assistive Actions
dimension.description: Assistive Actions encompass actions that one player performs to the benefit of other/s (i.e. note that the player can have indirect benefits such as reviving others to increase their own chances of success). In these games, players can support and assist other players in achieving their objectives.

dimensionExamples.example: Players share resources like jungle camps, buffs, and neutral objectives, as they provide significant advantages, such as gold, experience, and powerful buffs that benefit the entire team ( For example, Baron Nashor and dragons)

dimension.title: Interactables
dimension.description: Interactables refer to virtual objects and non-player characters/entities within the environment that respond to players’ actions. Interactables can be moved, shaped, or activated (e.g., a cannon that shoots when the player interacts with it). In some cases, interactables are also consumable (e.g., food in Overcooked is transported and modified as an interactable, but also consumed to complete the recipes). Interactables are shared when their state and attributes can be affected by more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: Players share the game map, which includes lanes, jungle areas, and objectives

dimension.title: Space
dimension.description: Space is also a resource as it defines the various places in the environment that a player can occupy and interact with. Space is shared when its utilisation is affected or constrained by others' presence or by others’ actions.

dimensionExamples.example: Champions in League of Legends have unique abilities, leading to an asymmetry in playstyles. For example, some champions specialize in damage, while others provide healing, shielding, or crowd control

dimension.title: Abilities
dimension.description: Abilities, as described by Harris et al. 2016, are where one player can do things another player cannot. In games where these actions synergise or are complementary, it incentivises collaboration.

dimensionExamples.example: Items and kills are an example of asymmetric usefulness, as kills and gold are often more valuable on carries like ADCs or mid laners than on tanks or support. Buffs like blue buff are more useful to champions that have mana opposed to champions who don't use mana

dimension.title: Usefulness
dimension.description: Usefulness happens when a certain resource or information (shared among multiple players) is more valuable  to one of those players. It can promote collaboration and coordination to maximise player performance/enjoyment.

dimensionExamples.example: Certain champions' abilities work exceptionally well together, allowing players to create powerful combos

dimension.title: Synergies
dimension.description: Synergies extended from Rocha et. al 2008 allow one entity to assist or change the game actions (e.g. abilities) of another.

dimensionExamples.example: Champions with different roles and strengths complement each other. For example, a tank absorbs damage while a damage dealer focuses on eliminating enemies, making both more effective when they work together

dimension.title: Complementarity
dimension.description: Complementarity, extended from Rocha et. al rocha2008game, corresponds to when player actions are designed to balance each other’s weaknesses or so that strengths complement each other. It is typically achieved through asymmetric game design, with each player bringing something to the shared experience.
